speakers: Tom Roble (co-host, SG CTA index / CTA research, London)
summary: Aug 2026 Systematic Investor: CTAs had an exceptional 12 months (SG CTA +23%) from diverse trends (equities, metals, energy, short gold); the group debates crisis alpha vs all-weather, trend vs non-trend CTAs, managed accounts and portable alpha, leverage lessons from the Situational Awareness fund, and survivorship/selection bias in CTA indices. Beer argues short-term models are a zero-Sharpe exercise and that trend alpha comes from humans failing to act on changes.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I don't know how you conduct any kind of normal traditional valuation
claims.claim: Traditional valuation analysis seems unusable in current equity markets, which resemble venture capital with fantastical projections (SpaceX IPO), possibly a repeat of 2000.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: this everinccreasing level of interest rates, right? The yields are just ticking higher and higher.
claims.claim: Rising yields are gradually ticking higher and are not getting enough attention.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's gone down to 27 which actually to to Andrew's point I think it was um it suggests that at the moment there are very few markets that are trending.
claims.claim: Trend barometer at 27 means only 27% of tracked markets are trending, so the opportunity set is limited though trend followers can still make money; profits came from equities, metals and a few currencies.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: most CTAs are still holding on to some strong year-to- date gains.
claims.claim: 2026 CTA gains came from precious metals early, energies when the Iran war began, and slow equity drift, i.e. from many places not a single trend; a trend model went short gold.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the suction CT index is up 23% over the past year. 23%, right?
claims.claim: SG CTA index +23% over 12 months with beta 0.3, versus MSCI World +21% and bonds +2%; being long equities after Liberation Day was contrarian tactical alpha.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: everything's kind of pointing in the same direction. And so when you get an event like an SVB or a liberation day or something that that reverberates
claims.claim: When one macro theme dominates and all CTA positions point the same way, a shock like SVB or Liberation Day produces the largest whipsaws.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: diversification is the only free lunch. And the way people and CCTAs allocate risk across markets really is paying dividends this year.
claims.claim: CTAs actively allocate risk across markets (not static allocation), which made 2026 returns resilient and systematic trading more palatable.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the fact that the damage wasn't worse was incredible, right? I mean it was I mean the yen has been one of the very best money makers
claims.claim: Yen intervention caused little damage to CTAs despite crowded short-yen exposure; Beer's 10-market portfolio even outperformed in those days.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: flat has been the new up like like where stability has been so valuable over the past four or five months.
claims.claim: Being long crude oil offset the war shock to long equities and long gold; stability has been the new up in 2026.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they underperformed by 4 or 500 basis points in 2022
claims.claim: Mutual fund CTAs underperformed hedge-fund CTAs by 400-500bp in 2022 due to 40 Act vol controls, but the gap has largely disappeared as clean low-fee funds replaced old products.
claims.indicator: UCITS/mutual fund CTA index vs SG CTA

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: that it had a unsurprisingly very high correlation to the main CTA index, enter trend followers. Um, but it seemed to have some structural kind of underperformance in terms of about 200 basis points per year
claims.claim: Mutual fund CTA index correlated highly with main index but underperformed by about 200bp a year due to structuring costs and untradeable markets.
claims.indicator: CTA mutual fund index vs SG CTA

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: when you do trade commodities in a uses fund it takes an extra couple of days to settle the P&L
claims.claim: UCITS commodity P&L settles with a lag, making daily comparisons with other vehicles unreliable; use weekly data to avoid time-zone and settlement mismatches.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: there may be more um carry going on in some funds
claims.claim: Some UCITS CTAs run non-trend carry, which hurts during carry unwinds (August 2024, July 2026), making them differ from pure trend.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: standard options pricing theory doesn't work well when you don't have normal distributions.
claims.claim: In fundamental commodity trading (e.g. natural gas with step-function costs from coal to gas) distributions are non-normal and information asymmetries are large.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: commodity enhanced beta in our in our capro world
claims.claim: Newer active commodity funds blend trend, carry and curve strategies to mitigate roll costs of being long commodities and provide inflation protection.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: The draws of commodities over the past 25 years is 80%.
claims.claim: Long-only commodities had an 80% max drawdown over 25 years versus below 20% for CTAs, which is why commodities get a small allocation.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the fear of CTAs is is there's a major whips on the market and we all lose 5% in a week.
claims.claim: CTA losses are small compared with levered discretionary funds (Situational Awareness, a roughly $45bn AI fund at 4:1 leverage that fell 67% in July).
claims.conditions: borrowing against collateral that can be liquidated

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the difference between borrowing money from somebody
claims.claim: Collateralised borrowing forces unwinds in drawdowns, whereas liquid futures with notional leverage do not; no CTA has suffered a Situational-Awareness-type loss.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they launched a 5:1 version of it or 3:1 or 4:1 or 5:1 and that fund ended up going down something like 90%.
claims.claim: A 5x leveraged version of a good CTA lost about 90% when a normal 20% drawdown occurred, showing leverage destroys capital.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: investors are increasingly looking at ways to be much more efficient in the way they access markets
claims.claim: SMA usage keeps growing, offering capital efficiency (margin only), cross-margining, liquidity, transparency and customisation.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it was probably much more about the risk management that they brought to the table. Not so much whether it's a 100 day breakout or it's a vault breakout or whatever
claims.claim: A paper on the Turtles' maths suggests risk management, not the entry breakout length, was the key edge of trend followers.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I wonder sometimes when we overengineer things they don't necessarily become better with time
claims.claim: Overengineering capital efficiency (portable alpha, more leverage) does not make strategies better and may be a risk.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: more and more instruments and the sharp ratio hasn't budged.
claims.claim: Over 25 years of extra engineering and instruments the CTA Sharpe ratio has not improved.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: you can get your CTA or your managed account allocation sometimes for quote unquote free without a capital cost
claims.claim: Managed accounts and portable alpha let investors overlay CTA exposure on top of 100% equities using futures margin, without selling equities.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: CTA as CTA trend, which I think most people are pretty familiar with, and then CTA non-trend.
claims.claim: SG splits CTAs into trend (dominated by large blue-chip firms) and non-trend (short-term, quant macro, commodity specialists), with non-trend niche or blending into quant multi-strats.
claims.indicator: SG CTA vs trend vs non-trend split

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: short-term CTAs have always been and continue to be a really challenging space.
claims.claim: Short-term CTAs struggle (Quest returned capital; Crabel is a rare survivor).

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: as soon as you change a parameter by a tiny amount, it it completely changes the way that the portfolio comes out.
claims.claim: Short-term strategies are highly parameter dependent, i.e. fragile.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: I was expecting trend following to be a reducing strategy and quant macro to be a much more obvious area of growth
claims.claim: Quant macro (fundamental forward-looking data) was expected to grow versus trend but many such groups closed.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there was a firm a few years ago that came out saying, "Oh, we can do this trend stuff for 50 basis point and they raised a billions of dollars very quickly
claims.claim: Calling trend 'plain vanilla' invites cheap, undifferentiated products which then failed.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the portfolios don't move. I mean, it's they they just don't move.
claims.claim: Alpha exists because most investors' strategic portfolios (60/40, sovereign funds) barely change, while trend followers hunt for changes outside their expectations.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's very very hard for humans to to to give up on their favorite ideas and their best ideas.
claims.claim: Humans hold losers with a white-knuckle grip; the ruthless rules-based exit is a money-generating alpha source.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I think it's about being very very early into a trend at the when the when the when this you know the signs of a trend begin to emerge.
claims.claim: Trend following is about being early at the first signs of a trend rather than late.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's a compliment. it completion strategy for something that you as an allocator don't do well which is to time the markets.
claims.claim: Trend following is a completion strategy for market timing that allocators cannot do themselves; the alpha worked in the past year without a crisis.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: investors continue to expect it to always be a case and so they get increasingly upset um when it doesn't always protect
claims.claim: Crisis alpha marketing creates disappointment when trend funds do not protect over short equity drawdowns, because trends take time to adapt; the rhetoric moved to risk mitigating strategies and all-weather.
claims.conditions: equity drawdown within a strong uptrend

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's on cash plus 250 basis points net of fees and expenses
claims.claim: SG CTA index earned about cash plus 250bp over 25 years; lumpy alpha means it earns cash in most years and large returns every 8-10 years.
claims.indicator: SG CTA index excess over cash

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the only way you solve that and you turn it to an all-weather portfolio is by bumping the sharp ratio up
claims.claim: To be all-weather and not 'dead money', CTAs must raise Sharpe, e.g. 40 points over cash in 10 years instead of 20.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: One is that it's it's unbiased. The other thing is it's highly liquid. So we can change exposure in no time and and and and it's opportunistic.
claims.claim: Original crisis alpha rationale (Katy Kaminski): trend following is unbiased, liquid and opportunistic.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: I think about half of the funds or strategies that report their performance to us for the indices are some sort of composite of a managed account. So, they won't include a cash rate.
claims.claim: Roughly half of CTA index contributors report managed-account composites with no cash return, biasing the index downward when rates are high.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a fund that has grown in size because they've done really well but but but we don't capture that positive lift anywhere.
claims.claim: Index reconstitution drops underperformers late and adds winners only after they are large, so the index captures their weaker large-scale performance and misses their growth phase.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: if you take the current 10 constituents of our trend index let's call it the 2026 vintage and then backfill
claims.claim: Backfilling current index constituents gives much stronger history (survivorship bias), as in Efficient Capital's 'Blinded by Bias'.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: 17 of the 20 have outperformed the index over the past 10 years
claims.claim: 17 of 20 current SG CTA constituents beat the index over 10 years (index at 15th percentile, Sharpe at 35th percentile), making manager selection look easy and understating single-manager risk; only 9 of 20 from 10 years ago still exist.
claims.indicator: SG CTA index vs current constituents

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: pick two or three or four that are structurally different, right? They're not all the same.
claims.claim: Allocate to two to four structurally different trend managers rather than one.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: It's a zero sharp ratio exercise.
claims.claim: Beer's research finds short-term models add no Sharpe: they look better on a graph but get whipsawed and overtrade; the trend sub-index has the same Sharpe as the broad index, so non-trend adds little diversification.
claims.indicator: short-term models; SG Trend sub-index vs SG CTA

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: that's no different than fall controls or uh you know or stop losses or other things that are designed to basically get you out of positions faster
claims.claim: Short-term models sold after 2022 as protection at inflection points act like vol controls or stop-losses, reducing drawdowns at a true economic cost of lost returns.
